output.title: Consent is not the same as evidence
output.body:
If you ever want to use a customer story, consent is only one part of the check. It answers who agreed to be quoted. It does not answer the harder question: does the wording stay inside what was actually done, and does it avoid hinting at results or capabilities you have not shown?

That matters because a testimonial can drift from permission into promotion. Someone may be fine with their name or quote being used, but that does not mean they approved every channel, every edit, or every implied outcome. A story about a pilot is still a pilot. It is not proof of scale, ROI, or a finished system unless those points are explicitly supported.

The practical next step is simple: before any story is published, write down three things in plain English — what was actually done, what the person agreed could be said, and what claims are off limits. Then compare the draft against those three lines. If the copy reads like a guarantee, it needs another pass. Human approval should stay in the loop before anything goes public. That is the boring part, which is usually the useful part.
